z-m-06-01.title: If the hour hand is near 5, is it 5 o'clock?
z-m-06-01.topic: Clock: reading the time with the hour hand and minute hand
z-m-06-01.goal: Know that the hour hand alone makes it hard to decide what hour it is and that you must read it together with the minute hand, and make your own examples of times when the hour hand is near 5 but it is not yet 5 o'clock.
z-m-06-01.material: An analog clock has an hour hand (the hand that tells the hour) and a minute hand (the hand that tells the minutes). When the minute hand points to 12 it is exactly on the hour, and each number space is 5 minutes. The clock numbers are 1 to 12. Jiho can't see the clock picture directly and plays a game of guessing the time from what a friend tells him in words. Whether it is a.m. or p.m. does not matter.
z-m-06-01.thinking.0: Postpone judgment or add conditions when information is not enough
z-m-06-01.thinking.1: Revise your judgment each time new information arrives
z-m-06-01.thinking.2: Make your own examples of easily confused cases
z-m-06-01.prereq.0: Reading on-the-hour and 5-minute times on an analog clock (Grade 2 level)
z-m-06-01.s.s1.prompt: Read what your friend says one piece at a time, and each time choose the time you can say right now.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.hint.0: Before new information comes, first say in one sentence how far your judgment is certain.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.hint.1: When new information comes, read separately what the hour hand and the minute hand each tell.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.0.info: The friend said, "The hour hand is very close to 5. I won't tell you about the minute hand yet."
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: What time can you say now?
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.0.after: The hour hand being near 5 can appear just before 5, like 4:50, or just after 5 o'clock. So asking more about the minute hand and just guessing 'around 5 o'clock' are both fine.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It's 5 o'clock. The number the hour hand is close to is 5.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You read the number the hour hand is close to directly as the hour. You decided even though you don't know the minute hand yet.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It could be around 4 o'clock or around 5 o'clock. I need to know the minute hand.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You considered that the hour hand could be just before 5 or just past 5.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It seems to be 5 o'clock but I can't be sure. I'll ask more about the minute hand.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is the idea of guessing with the clues you have now, not being sure, and trying to find out more.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It's 4 o'clock. The hour hand hasn't reached 5 yet.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You decided on 4 just from it not having reached 5. You didn't consider whether it could be just past 5.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.1.info: The friend said, "The minute hand points to 10."
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: What time is it now, in hours and minutes?
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.1.after: If the minute hand points to 10, it is 50 minutes. Around 50 minutes, even if the hour hand is almost touching the next number 5, it is not yet 5 o'clock, so it is 4:50. Saying it is 10 minutes before 5 o'clock is the same time.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Reading the minute hand's 10 as 50 minutes is right. But you decided the hour from the number 5 the hour hand is close to.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You read the number 10 that the minute hand points to directly as 10 minutes. Recall again how many minutes each number space is.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You read the minutes from the minute hand and the hour from the fact that the hour hand has not yet reached 5.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You read the hour as 4, but you read the minute hand's number 10 directly as minutes.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.2.info: It's a new problem. The friend said, "This time the hour hand has just passed 5, and the minute hand points to 2."
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: What time is this, in hours and minutes?
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.2.after: The hour hand has just passed 5, so it is a little after 5 o'clock, and the minute hand's 2 is 10 minutes. The hour hand tells the hour and the minute hand tells the minutes.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Reading the minute hand's 2 as 10 minutes is right. But you missed that the hour hand has already passed 5.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You read the hour from the number the hour hand has passed and the minutes from the number the minute hand points to, separately.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You read the minute hand's number 2 directly as 2 minutes.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You read the minute hand's number 2 as 20 minutes. Check again how many minutes each number space is.
z-m-06-01.s.s1.reflect: At first, from the hour hand alone, you could guess 'around 5 o'clock' or ask more. When the new information, the minute hand, came, it showed that even the hour could change. You can't say that the number the hour hand is close to is the same as the current hour.
z-m-06-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different times when the hour hand is closer to 5 than to 4 but it is not yet 5 o'clock. The minute hand points exactly at a number (the minutes are a multiple of 5). Write the hour as h and the minutes as m. (Example: for 7:15, h=7, m=15)
z-m-06-01.s.s2.hint.0: Choose the hour as the one that is not 5, and choose the minutes from multiples of 5.
z-m-06-01.s.s2.hint.1: Suppose that at 4:30 the hour hand is exactly halfway between 4 and 5, and compare how the minutes must differ to go closer toward 5.
z-m-06-01.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a time in the 4 o'clock hour.
z-m-06-01.s.s2.fail.c1: It must be before 5 o'clock, so set the hour to 4.
z-m-06-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The minutes are where the minute hand points exactly at a number.
z-m-06-01.s.s2.fail.c2: Set the minutes to a multiple of 5 that is at least 0 and less than 60.
z-m-06-01.s.s2.ok.c3: The hour hand is closer to 5 than to 4.
z-m-06-01.s.s2.fail.c3: 4:30 is halfway between 4 and 5. To be closer to 5, the minutes must be greater.
z-m-06-01.s.s2.explain: 4:35, 4:40, 4:45, 4:50, and 4:55 are all right examples. 4:30 is halfway between 4 and 5, so it was left out under this condition. The greater the minutes, the closer the hour hand gets to 5, but it is 5 o'clock only when the minute hand has gone all the way around and come to 12.
z-m-06-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Even though the hour hand is close to 5, explain why it is not 5 o'clock, using one of the times you just made as an example.
z-m-06-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: Say one of the times you chose out loud, and write which number the minute hand is on at that time.
z-m-06-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Recall where the minute hand must be at exactly 5 o'clock, and compare it with the current time.
z-m-06-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write exactly the number or minutes the minute hand points to in your example?
z-m-06-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write knowing that 'the hour hand is near' and 'that hour has arrived' are different things?
z-m-06-01.s.s2.because.model.0: If the minute hand points to 10, it is 50 minutes. For it to be 5 o'clock, the minute hand must go around once more and come to 12, so right now it is still 4:50.
z-m-06-01.s.s2.because.model.1: The hour hand moves a little at a time as time goes on and gets close to 5. But if the minute hand hasn't come to 12 yet, like 4:40, it is still 4 o'clock.

z-m-06-02.title: What more do we need to know the length of strings tied together?
z-m-06-02.topic: Length: total length of tied-together strings (cm)
z-m-06-02.goal: Know that if you tie the ends of strings by overlapping them, the length is not simply the sum, say what information is needed to state the exact length, and make examples of possible lengths.
z-m-06-02.material: Hajun has string 가, which is 40cm long, and string 나, which is 35cm long. He overlapped the ends of the two strings a little and tied them to make one long string. The string is stretched straight to measure its length. Hajun said, "It's the two strings' lengths put together, so the tied string is 75cm." We don't yet know how many cm the overlapping part is.
z-m-06-02.thinking.0: Judge whether the given information is enough
z-m-06-02.thinking.2: Make several cases that fit the conditions
z-m-06-02.prereq.0: Reading length in cm and two-digit calculation (Grade 2 level)
z-m-06-02.s.s1.prompt: How can we look at what Hajun said?
z-m-06-02.s.s1.hint.0: Lay string 가 and string 나 out separately and look at which part is included in both strings when they are tied together.
z-m-06-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how many times the overlapping part should go into the total length.
z-m-06-02.s.s1.o.a: That's right. There are two strings, so you just add the lengths.
z-m-06-02.s.s1.r.a: You added the lengths as they are without using the condition that the strings were overlapped and tied.
z-m-06-02.s.s1.o.b: It's longer than 75cm. Tying makes the string longer.
z-m-06-02.s.s1.r.b: You thought tying makes it longer. Recall what happens when the ends of the strings overlap as you tie them.
z-m-06-02.s.s1.o.c: It's shorter than 75cm. It gets shorter by the amount that overlaps.
z-m-06-02.s.s1.r.c: You noticed that the overlapping part is in both strings once each but goes into the total length only once.
z-m-06-02.s.s1.o.d: Can't tell. This is because we don't know how thick the strings are.
z-m-06-02.s.s1.r.d: You thought information that has nothing to do with length was needed. Work out what information is really needed.
z-m-06-02.s.s1.explain: We overlapped and tied the ends, so the overlapping part is in both strings. So it is shorter than the combined 75cm by the overlapping length. To know how much shorter, we need to know the overlapping length.
z-m-06-02.s.s2.prompt: What would you need to know to decide the exact length of the tied string? Choose everything that lets you decide the exact length once you know it.
z-m-06-02.s.s2.hint.0: Think one by one about whether you can decide the tied string's length once you know each choice.
z-m-06-02.s.s2.hint.1: Look for whether there is a way to work out the length and a way to know the length directly.
z-m-06-02.s.s2.o.a: The colors of the two strings
z-m-06-02.s.s2.r.a: Color has nothing to do with length.
z-m-06-02.s.s2.o.b: The time it took to tie the strings
z-m-06-02.s.s2.r.b: Time doesn't tell you the length.
z-m-06-02.s.s2.o.c: The length of the overlapping part
z-m-06-02.s.s2.r.c: If you know the overlapping length, you can take that much off the lengths of the two strings.
z-m-06-02.s.s2.o.d: The length of the tied string, stretched straight and measured
z-m-06-02.s.s2.r.d: If you measure directly, you can know the total length right away without calculating.
z-m-06-02.s.s2.explain: If you know the overlapping length, or stretch the tied string straight and measure it directly, you can know the exact length. Knowing just one of the two is enough.
z-m-06-02.s.s2.acc.0: Choosing only the overlapping length can also decide the exact length. It is even better if you also think of the way of stretching it out and measuring directly.
z-m-06-02.s.s2.acc.1: Choosing only the direct measuring method can also tell the exact length. It is even better if you also think that you can calculate if you know the overlapping length.
z-m-06-02.s.s3.prompt: Say the overlapping length is at least 2cm and at most 7cm (a natural number). Make 2 different cases for what the total length of the tied string could be. Write the overlapping length as o and the total length of the tied string as t (unit cm).
z-m-06-02.s.s3.hint.0: Pick an overlapping length and work out how many times that part is included in the combined value of the two strings' lengths.
z-m-06-02.s.s3.hint.1: Write side by side in a table how the total length changes when the overlapping length you choose changes.
z-m-06-02.s.s3.var.t: Total length of the tied string (cm)
z-m-06-02.s.s3.ok.c1: The overlapping length is a natural number from 2cm to 7cm.
z-m-06-02.s.s3.fail.c1: Make the overlapping length a natural number from 2 to 7.
z-m-06-02.s.s3.ok.c2: The total length equals the combined length of the two strings minus the overlapping length.
z-m-06-02.s.s3.fail.c2: The total length is not right. Think again about what to do with the overlapping length from the combined length.
z-m-06-02.s.s3.explain: If the overlapping length is 2cm it is 73cm, if 3cm it is 72cm, and if 7cm it is 68cm. If the overlapping length changes, the total length changes too, so there are many possible lengths from 68cm to 73cm.
z-m-06-02.s.s4.prompt: How would it be good to correct Hajun's statement '75cm'? Also write why you correct it that way.
z-m-06-02.s.s4.hint.0: First sort out what is right and what is wrong in what Hajun said.
z-m-06-02.s.s4.hint.1: Recall the method you chose in the step above and write what to do to state the exact length.
z-m-06-02.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Did you write thinking about 'when Hajun's statement is right and when it is wrong'?
z-m-06-02.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Did you also include what you need to know to know the exact length?
z-m-06-02.s.s4.model.0: It might not be 75cm. We overlapped and tied the two strings, so it gets shorter by the overlapping length. If you know how many cm the overlapping part is, subtract it from 75.
z-m-06-02.s.s4.model.1: Stretch the tied string straight and measure it with a ruler. There is an overlapping part, so it will come out shorter than 75cm.

z-m-06-03.title: Where should Soyul's plan for a building-block house be fixed?
z-m-06-03.topic: Unit cubes: number per floor and the rule for stacking
z-m-06-03.goal: Using the rule that blocks on an upper floor must be supported by blocks on the floor below, find the wrong part of a plan and make several plans that follow the rule.
z-m-06-03.material: A unit cube is a cube-shaped wooden block of one-space size. Soyul wants to build a house shape using all 7 unit cubes. The rules are as follows. (1) On floor 1, place the unit cubes in one line with no empty space. (2) Floor 2 unit cubes can be placed only directly on top of floor 1 unit cubes, and only one floor 2 block goes on each floor 1 block. (3) Do not build floor 3. Read Soyul's plan line by line.
z-m-06-03.thinking.0: Find where the plan breaks a rule
z-m-06-03.thinking.1: Make several ways that keep the conditions
z-m-06-03.prereq.0: Experience building floor 1 and floor 2 shapes with unit cubes (Grade 2 level)
z-m-06-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in Soyul's plan that doesn't follow the rules or is said wrongly.
z-m-06-03.s.s1.hint.0: Point, one by one, to where each floor 2 block sits on the floor 1 blocks.
z-m-06-03.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many places in all a floor 2 block can be placed on the 3 floor 1 blocks.
z-m-06-03.s.s1.line.1: I put 3 in a line on floor 1.
z-m-06-03.s.s1.line.2: I will put the remaining 4 on floor 2.
z-m-06-03.s.s1.line.3: 3+4=7, so it is a way to use all 7.
z-m-06-03.s.s1.line.4: So I can build the house with this plan.
z-m-06-03.s.s1.explain: Lines 3 and 5 are wrong. If you put 3 on floor 1, there are only 3 places for floor 2 blocks to go, but it said to put 4. The calculation in line 4 (3+4=7) is right. But the numbers adding up to 7 doesn't make it a plan that keeps the rules. So the conclusion in line 5 is wrong. If you chose an earlier line, check again whether those lines match the rules.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different plans that use all 7 unit cubes while keeping all the rules. Write the number placed on floor 1 as a and the number on floor 2 as b. Both floor 1 and floor 2 must have blocks.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.hint.0: First decide a number for floor 1 and check whether all the remaining blocks can go up on floor 2.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.hint.1: Change the floor 1 number and write it beside the floor 2 number, and look at what happens to rows where floor 2 has more than floor 1.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.ok.c1: Both floor 1 and floor 2 have a natural number of blocks.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Make both floor 1 and floor 2 a natural number of 1 or more.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The floor 1 and floor 2 blocks together must be 7.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.ok.c3: All floor 2 blocks can sit on floor 1 blocks.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.fail.c3: If there are more floor 2 blocks than floor 1 blocks, some blocks have nothing to support them.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.explain: The plans that keep the rules are 4 on floor 1 and 3 on floor 2, 5 on floor 1 and 2 on floor 2, and 6 on floor 1 and 1 on floor 2, 3 plans in all. A plan with more on floor 2, like 3 on floor 1 and 4 on floor 2, can't be made because there is nothing to support some blocks.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why Soyul's first plan (3 on floor 1, 4 on floor 2) doesn't work, and tell the relationship between the number of floor 2 blocks and the number of floor 1 blocks.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Pair up and write which floor 1 block each of the 4 floor 2 blocks sits on.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Recall what happens when a floor 2 block has no partner.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you include the point 'there must be one floor 1 block under each floor 2 block'?
z-m-06-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you compare the numbers of floor 1 and floor 2 blocks when you explained?
z-m-06-03.s.s2.because.model.0: Floor 2 blocks can be placed only directly on floor 1 blocks, and with 3 on floor 1 there are only 3 places. So you can't put 4 on floor 2. The number of floor 2 blocks can't be more than the number of floor 1 blocks.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.because.model.1: One of the 4 has no floor 1 block below to support it, so it would float in the air. So the number of floor 2 blocks must be equal to or less than floor 1.
z-m-06-03.s.s2.because.model.2: The 1st layer has 3 wood blocks, so you can put at most 3 on the 2nd layer. The 2nd layer must not have more than the 1st layer.

z-m-06-04.title: What if you measure the same hallway twice and the length is different?
z-m-06-04.topic: Length: values that differ when the same length is measured several times
z-m-06-04.goal: When the same length is measured several times and the values differ a little, examine the way of measuring and decide how to state the length.
z-m-06-04.material: We measure the length of the school hallway with a 1m stick. We mark the end of the stick with chalk, place the end of the stick against the marked spot again, and keep measuring. We measure the remaining part with a cm ruler and write it like '3m 40cm'. 1m is 100cm. We don't yet know the hallway's real length.
z-m-06-04.thinking.0: Examine how the way of measuring affects the result
z-m-06-04.thinking.1: Revise your judgment each time a new value comes
z-m-06-04.thinking.2: Write including how far it can be trusted
z-m-06-04.prereq.0: Know that 1m is 100cm and read lengths written with both m and cm (Grade 2 level)
z-m-06-04.s.s1.prompt: Each time a measurement result arrives, choose the judgment you can make now.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.hint.0: When a new value comes, change both to the same unit and compare how much it differs from the earlier value.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.hint.1: When the values differ, first ask how it was measured, and check whether the values measured the same way are close.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.0.info: Group A measured the hallway once and got 3m 40cm.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: How would it be good to state the length of the hallway?
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.0.after: A value measured once is precious evidence, but it is too early to say 'exactly this much.' Suggesting measuring again is fine, and writing it down as 'about' is also fine.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You called a value measured once the exact length. You haven't checked that measuring again would give the same value.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Take it as about 3m 40cm, and measure once more to check.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You used the current value as your basis and also thought of a way to check.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: A value measured once can't be trusted, so throw it away.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You even threw away a value you could use. A value measured once is also precious evidence.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: For now, write it down as about 3m 40cm.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: By writing 'about,' you left the point that it may not be exact yet.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Group B measured the same hallway again and got 3m 46cm.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: What do you think when you see the two values (3m 40cm and 3m 46cm)?
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.1.after: If you subtract 3m 40cm from 3m 46cm, there is a 6cm difference. It is certain that values measured once differ by 6cm. Rather than saying one side is wrong, it is good to ask how they measured or to measure once more.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Group A's value is right, and Group B is wrong.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You don't know yet how they measured, but you decided one is right.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: They differ by 6cm, but we can't yet decide which is more trustworthy.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You saw the difference between the two values and noticed there is not yet a basis to decide.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The hallway got longer between the two times.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You thought the hallway length changed. Think about whether the way of measuring could make a difference.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The two values are close, so you can say both are about 3m 40cm. Measure once more.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Seeing that the two values differ by 6cm, you thought about the approximate length and the next action together.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.2.info: It turned out that Group A measured while marking the end of the stick with chalk each time, and Group B moved the stick without marking. If you move it without marking, the stick easily overlaps or leaves gaps. Group C measured again with marking and got 3m 41cm.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: How would it be good to sum up the hallway's length?
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.2.after: The two values measured with marking (3m 40cm, 3m 41cm) differ by only 1cm, so that method can be seen as more trustworthy. Still, rather than throwing away 3m 46cm completely, it is good to record that 'it may have differed because there was no marking.' Stating it as a range spread over the three values is also fine.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The longest, 3m 46cm, is the real one, and the others were measured too short.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You thought the larger value is always accurate. If the stick overlaps, it can actually come out longer.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The 3m 40cm and 3m 41cm measured with marking are close, so take it as about 3m 40cm, and find out more about why 3m 46cm was different.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You used as your basis that values measured the same way are close, and also looked into the reason for the other value.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The values differ each time we measure, so the hallway's length can't be known.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You said the length can't be known at all because the values differ a little. Look at whether the close values gather in one place.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Trust all three values and say the hallway is between 3m 40cm and 3m 46cm.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You didn't throw away any value and stated the range the values spread over.
z-m-06-04.s.s1.reflect: A value measured once could be used only as 'about,' and when the second value came, it showed there was a 6cm difference. When the new information, the way of measuring, came, there was a basis to say which value is more trustworthy. Rather than trusting one value as accurate, it is good to look together at where the values gather and at the method.
z-m-06-04.s.s2.prompt: You want to write the hallway length on a notice board. Write how it would be good to write it, and give one reason for writing it that way.
z-m-06-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write the three measured values side by side and group the most similar values together.
z-m-06-04.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the words you wrote let the reader know how much to trust this value.
z-m-06-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write the length so that the reader won't misunderstand it as 'exactly this much'?
z-m-06-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did your reason come from the way of measuring or from the differences in the values?
z-m-06-04.s.s2.model.0: The hallway length is about 3m 40cm. This is because the two measurements made with marking were nearly the same, 3m 40cm and 3m 41cm.
z-m-06-04.s.s2.model.1: The hallway length is between 3m 40cm and 3m 46cm. We measured three times and the values differed a little each time.

z-m-06-05.title: If you stick two triangle pieces together, is it a hexagon?
z-m-06-05.topic: Triangles and quadrilaterals: number of sides of a shape made by sticking pieces together
z-m-06-05.goal: Know that the number of sides of a shape made by sticking two triangle pieces together can differ depending on how they are stuck, and find and fix the wrong part in Sora's thinking.
z-m-06-05.material: There are 2 paper pieces shaped like right triangles. The two have exactly the same size and shape. The two sides next to the right angle are 3cm and 4cm, and the longest side is 5cm. A right angle is a square corner, and if you join two right angles, they become one straight line with no bend. Stick the two together exactly along one side, with no overlap and no gap, to make one shape. It is even better to cut out the paper and try it yourself. Read Sora's thinking line by line.
z-m-06-05.thinking.0: Examine what happens to the stuck sides
z-m-06-05.thinking.1: Test the phrase 'however you stick them'
z-m-06-05.thinking.2: Argue against it with an example
z-m-06-05.prereq.0: Sides and right angles of triangles, quadrilaterals, and hexagons (Grade 2 level)
z-m-06-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in Sora's thinking that is not correct.
z-m-06-05.s.s1.hint.1: Picture the shape made by sticking two paper pieces along one side, and count the sides you can see on the outside one by one.
z-m-06-05.s.s1.line.0: A triangle piece has 3 sides each.
z-m-06-05.s.s1.line.1: There are two, so there are 3+3=6 sides in all.
z-m-06-05.s.s1.line.2: When you stick two together, the two stuck sides can't be seen from outside.
z-m-06-05.s.s1.line.3: So the shape made by sticking has 6 sides.
z-m-06-05.s.s1.line.4: It has 6 sides, so however you stick them, it becomes a hexagon.
z-m-06-05.s.s1.explain: Lines 4 and 5 are not correct. Line 3 said the two stuck sides can't be seen from outside, so the sides seen on the outside are 6 minus those two. But line 4 didn't reflect that. The 6 in line 2 is right as the number of sides before sticking. If you chose an earlier line, tell apart whether those lines are about before sticking or after sticking.
z-m-06-05.s.s2.prompt: This time, stick the 4cm sides together, but flip one piece over so the two right-angle corners meet at one point. If you count sides seen on the outside that are joined in one line as one side, what shape is the shape made by sticking?
z-m-06-05.s.s2.hint.0: Picture what shape the two 3cm sides make where the two right-angle corners meet.
z-m-06-05.s.s2.hint.1: Go once around the sides you can see on the outside and point to them, counting those joined in one line only once.
z-m-06-05.s.s2.r.a: You thought of the two stuck sides disappearing, but you missed that two sides joined in one line look like a single side.
z-m-06-05.s.s2.r.b: You thought together about the stuck sides disappearing and counting sides joined in one line as one side.
z-m-06-05.s.s2.r.c: It seems you counted one extra while counting the remaining sides. Go once around the outside and point to them one by one.
z-m-06-05.s.s2.r.d: You used the number of sides from before sticking as it is. Look again at what happens to the stuck sides.
z-m-06-05.s.s2.explain: The two stuck 4cm sides go inside and can't be seen. The remaining sides are two 3cm sides and two 5cm sides. But since two right angles met, the two 3cm sides become one straight line, one 6cm side. So it is a triangle with 3 sides.
z-m-06-05.s.s3.prompt: Tell Sora why 'however you stick them, it becomes a hexagon' is not right. Use the way of sticking you just looked at as an example.
z-m-06-05.s.s3.hint.0: You may use the same way of counting the sides of the shape that you used in the last step.
z-m-06-05.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what one example would make the phrase 'however you stick them' wrong.
z-m-06-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you count the sides seen on the outside one by one in your example?
z-m-06-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write knowing that one example breaks the phrase 'however you stick them'?
z-m-06-05.s.s3.model.0: It isn't always a hexagon. The stuck sides can't be seen from outside, and if you stick the 4cm sides together, it can become a triangle.
z-m-06-05.s.s3.model.1: It depends on how you stick them. If you stick the 5cm sides together, it becomes a quadrilateral with 4 sides.
z-m-06-05.s.s1.hint.0: Separate whether each line is about before sticking them together or after sticking them together.
z-m-06-05.s.s3.model.2: If you stick the 5 cm sides together, it becomes a quadrilateral, so it is not a hexagon.
z-m-06-05.s.s3.model.3: If you stick the 4 cm sides together so that the two right-angle corners meet, it becomes a triangle with 3 sides. So however you stick them, it is not a hexagon.

z-m-06-06.title: From how many cm is a pencil 'long'?
z-m-06-06.topic: Classification: setting a criterion clearly with numbers
z-m-06-06.goal: Set a classification criterion that can differ from person to person, like 'long pencil,' clearly with a number such as length (cm), and know that several criteria are possible for the same data.
z-m-06-06.material: We measured the lengths of 8 pencils and they were 9cm, 11cm, 12cm, 14cm, 15cm, 17cm, 18cm, and 20cm. All lengths were measured in natural numbers (cm) and are different from each other. Jinseo wants to divide these pencils into two groups, 'long pencils' and 'short pencils.' At first Jinseo decided, 'Long pencils are pencils that look long, and short pencils are pencils that look short.'
z-m-06-06.thinking.0: Judge whether the classification criterion is clear
z-m-06-06.thinking.1: Make a criterion that fits the conditions yourself
z-m-06-06.thinking.2: Know that different criteria can make the same result
z-m-06-06.prereq.0: Reading lengths measured in cm and comparing the sizes of numbers (Grade 2 level)
z-m-06-06.s.s1.prompt: What problem does Jinseo's first criterion have?
z-m-06-06.s.s1.hint.0: Place the 8 pencils in order of length and point to up to where they are definitely long pencils.
z-m-06-06.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether you and a friend would each put a pencil in the middle on the same side if you divided them separately.
z-m-06-06.s.s1.o.a: The numbers of long pencils and short pencils are not the same.
z-m-06-06.s.s1.r.a: You mixed up the criterion for dividing with the numbers in the result of dividing. The two groups don't have to have equal numbers.
z-m-06-06.s.s1.o.b: We didn't measure the pencil lengths in cm.
z-m-06-06.s.s1.r.b: Measuring lengths is good, but even if you know the lengths, the same problem remains if you don't decide from where 'long' starts.
z-m-06-06.s.s1.o.c: There are only 8 pencils, so we can't divide them.
z-m-06-06.s.s1.r.c: Even with few pencils you can divide them into two groups. The problem is not the number but the criterion.
z-m-06-06.s.s1.r.d: You pointed out that if the criterion is not clear, the result changes depending on who divides.
z-m-06-06.s.s1.explain: 'Looks long' can feel different to different people. A pencil in the middle, like the 15cm pencil, can go on either side depending on the person, so we need a criterion that gives the same result no matter who divides.
z-m-06-06.s.s2.prompt: Set the criterion 'a pencil is long if its length is c cm or more' so that the result is the same no matter who divides. Make the long pencils 3 or more and 5 or fewer, and make the short pencils 3 or more too (c is a natural number). If the pencils are divided the same way even when c differs, count it as one way. Make 2 values of c that give different divisions.
z-m-06-06.s.s2.hint.0: Write the pencils in order of length and find where to draw a line so that the long side has 3 to 5 pencils.
z-m-06-06.s.s2.hint.1: Move the line one space at a time and count how the number of long pencils changes.
z-m-06-06.s.s2.ok.c1: c is a natural number of 1 or more.
z-m-06-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Make c a natural number of 1 or more.
z-m-06-06.s.s2.ok.c2: There are 3 or more long pencils.
z-m-06-06.s.s2.fail.c2: There are fewer than 3 long pencils. Try a smaller criterion.
z-m-06-06.s.s2.ok.c3: There are 5 or fewer long pencils, so there are also 3 or more short pencils.
z-m-06-06.s.s2.fail.c3: There are more than 5 long pencils. Try a larger criterion so that there are 3 or more short pencils.
z-m-06-06.s.s2.explain: If c is 13 or 14, the 14cm, 15cm, 17cm, 18cm, and 20cm pencils are long (5 pencils), if c is 15, there are 4 pencils of 15cm or more, and if c is 16 or 17, there are 3 pencils of 17cm or more. All c from 13 to 17 are possible, but there are three ways the pencils are divided.
z-m-06-06.s.s3.prompt: Tell one way your criterion is better than Jinseo's first criterion ('pencils that look long').
z-m-06-06.s.s3.hint.0: Picture how people would differ in dividing the 15cm pencil with Jinseo's first criterion.
z-m-06-06.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether, with your criterion, the 15cm pencil goes on the same side no matter who divides.
z-m-06-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: With the number you set, can you say right away which side the 15cm pencil is on?
z-m-06-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: If a friend uses your criterion, does the same result come out?
z-m-06-06.s.s3.model.0: If you set it as 14cm or more, the same result comes out no matter who divides. If you decide by eye, people can divide differently.
z-m-06-06.s.s3.model.1: If you set the criterion with a number, there is no confusion about whether the 15cm pencil is long or short, so it is clear.

z-m-06-07.title: Can we describe our class from the results of asking on the playground?
z-m-06-07.topic: Survey: whom you asked and the survey results
z-m-06-07.goal: Know that when reading survey results, not only how many people you asked but also whom you asked matters, and revise judgment and confidence with new information.
z-m-06-07.material: We are surveying 24 students in Class 3 about the one sport they like best. The choices are soccer, dodgeball, and jump rope, and each person picks only one. Hangyeol asked 12 friends he met on the playground during break.
z-m-06-07.thinking.0: Distinguish the range of people surveyed from the whole class
z-m-06-07.thinking.1: Revise judgment and confidence with new information
z-m-06-07.prereq.0: Sorting data, counting, and comparing more and less (Grade 2 level)
z-m-06-07.s.s1.prompt: Each time a survey result and new news arrive, choose the judgment you can make now.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.hint.0: Look at whether the people surveyed were all friends in the same place doing the same thing.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.hint.1: Think separately about whether newly learned facts change the numbers in the result or change how much to trust it.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.0.info: The result of Hangyeol asking 12 people is soccer 9, dodgeball 2, and jump rope 1.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think now about the sport the 24 students in Class 3 like best?
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.0.after: Among the 12, soccer is the most. But we don't yet know how the other 12 choose. So it is too early to decide for the whole class.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Soccer is the most. 9 of 12 chose it, so the whole class is the same.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You directly extended the result of the 12 asked to the result for the whole class. We don't know about the other 12 yet.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Among the 12 asked, soccer is the most. For the whole class, we need to know the rest too.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You spoke separately about the range surveyed and the whole class.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Only 12 people, so nothing can be said.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The result of the 12 surveyed is also usable evidence. You can say as much as you can say.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Soccer looks ahead, but we don't know the other 12, so I'll keep it only as a guess and find out more.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is the idea of guessing with the current result, not being sure, and trying to find out more.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.1.info: Recalling where Hangyeol asked, all 12 were friends playing soccer on the playground. Nobody asked the friends in the classroom.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: Knowing this, what happens to your first judgment?
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.1.after: If you ask friends who were playing soccer, many are likely to choose soccer. So it became harder to trust it as the result for the whole class. Lowering your confidence is fine, and asking more of the friends in the classroom is fine too.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.1.o.a: My first judgment stays the same. 9 people chose it, so soccer is the most.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You didn't examine how the newly learned fact affects your judgment.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.1.o.b: I keep the thought that soccer is the most, but my confidence has gone down.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You did not change your thought and revised how much to trust it.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.1.o.c: He asked as many as 12 people, so where he asked doesn't matter.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You looked only at how many people and missed whom he asked.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.1.o.d: He asked only friends playing soccer, so throw this result away.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You even threw away the point that this result tells what those 12 think.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.1.r.e: You found who was left out of the survey.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.2.info: The next day Hangyeol asked all 24 (including the first 12). The result is soccer 10, dodgeball 8, and jump rope 6.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.2.after: This time the whole class was surveyed, so we can say soccer 10, dodgeball 8, and jump rope 6. Among the first 12, soccer was 9, but in all it is 10, so only 1 of the 12 outside the playground chose soccer. Even though the result came out as soccer again, we could not have known that from the first survey alone.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.2.o.a: In the result of surveying all 24, soccer is the most.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You read the result of surveying the whole class.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The first survey was right. It was the same soccer, so where he asked doesn't matter.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You thought the first survey method was trustworthy because the result became the same.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The friends who chose soccer are more than half of the 24.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Half of 24 is 12. Check whether 10 is more than half.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Among the first 12 it was 9, but in all it is only 10, so only 1 of the 12 outside the playground chose soccer.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You compared the first survey result with the new result and worked out what the friends who were left out think.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.reflect: At first, from the result of 12, we could only 'guess.' When we learned whom he asked, our confidence went down even for the same result. Even though the final result came out on the same side (soccer) as at first, it does not change that the first survey alone could not have shown that.
z-m-06-07.s.s2.prompt: Write whom and how Hangyeol should ask the next time he surveys, together with the reason for doing so.
z-m-06-07.s.s2.hint.0: Recall where the friends left out of the first survey were.
z-m-06-07.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the method you chose gathers only friends who easily choose a certain sport.
z-m-06-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is it a method that gathers friends who resemble the whole class?
z-m-06-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check that your method does not gather only friends who like one sport?
z-m-06-07.s.s2.model.0: I should ask all 24 classmates. If I ask only friends on the playground, they easily choose soccer and the result leans to one side.
z-m-06-07.s.s2.model.1: I will ask friends in many places evenly, like the classroom, the playground, and the hallway. That way, only friends who like one sport won't gather.
z-m-06-07.s.s1.st.1.o.e: The first result alone makes it hard to speak for the whole class, so we should also ask the friends who were in the classroom.
z-m-06-07.s.s2.model.2: If you hand out the questionnaire to the whole class, you can find out what every friend thinks.

z-m-06-08.title: I drew a marble 5 times and got red 4 times. What might be in the bag?
z-m-06-08.topic: Possibility: guessing what is in the bag from the drawn results
z-m-06-08.goal: From the drawn results, state several cases that could be in the bag, and tell apart 'cases that can happen' from 'cases that are more likely.'
z-m-06-08.material: There are 8 marbles in all in the bag. The marbles are only red marbles and blue marbles. You can't see inside, so you took out one marble, looked at its color, put it back, and mixed well, and did this 5 times. The result is red 4 times and blue 1 time. Yunha said, "There must be more red marbles in there." and Daon said, "There could be just 1 blue marble, couldn't there?"
z-m-06-08.thinking.0: Tell apart cases that can and cannot happen
z-m-06-08.thinking.1: Make several cases that fit the conditions
z-m-06-08.thinking.2: Distinguish what is certain from what is a guess
z-m-06-08.prereq.0: Splitting a number up to 8 into two numbers and comparing more and less (Grade 2 level)
z-m-06-08.s.s1.prompt: When this result came out, choose all the ways the red and blue marbles in the bag could be.
z-m-06-08.s.s1.hint.1: Recall that the marble is put back after being taken out, and think about whether a color with fewer marbles can also come up many times.
z-m-06-08.s.s1.r.a: You missed that red came up once. If there are no red marbles at all, you can't draw one.
z-m-06-08.s.s1.r.b: You noticed that even if there is only 1 red marble, it can come up many times if it is put back and drawn again.
z-m-06-08.s.s1.r.c: You missed that blue came up once. If there are no blue marbles at all, you can't draw one.
z-m-06-08.s.s1.r.d: You chose a case where both colors are there and there are more red.
z-m-06-08.s.s1.explain: Red and blue both came up, so both colors must have 1 or more. So both 1 red and 7 blue, and 5 red and 3 blue are possible. It is only that the side with more red is more likely.
z-m-06-08.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different ways the bag could be that this result could come from. Write the number of red marbles as r and the number of blue marbles as b. There are 8 marbles in all.
z-m-06-08.s.s2.hint.0: First decide at least how many of each of the two colors must be in the bag.
z-m-06-08.s.s2.hint.1: Change the number of red marbles one at a time and write in a table what the number of blue marbles becomes.
z-m-06-08.s.s2.ok.c1: Both red and blue are 1 or more.
z-m-06-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Red and blue each came up once, so both colors must be 1 or more.
z-m-06-08.s.s2.fail.c2: Red and blue together must be 8.
z-m-06-08.s.s2.explain: All 7 cases are possible, from 1 red and 7 blue to 7 red and 1 blue. The side with more red is more likely, but what matters is that there is not just one possible case.
z-m-06-08.s.s2.because.prompt: Compare what Yunha said and what Daon said, and write your own thoughts.
z-m-06-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: Divide what the two said into what you can say for certain from the drawn result and what is a guess.
z-m-06-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think separately about whether Yunha's statement must be right and whether Daon's statement could happen.
z-m-06-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write separately what case each of the two is talking about?
z-m-06-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you tell apart 'what is certain' and 'what is a guess'?
z-m-06-08.s.s2.because.model.0: It seems there are more red marbles, but it's not certain. Like Daon said, there could be just 1 blue marble, and even if there is only 1 red marble, this kind of result can happen.
z-m-06-08.s.s2.because.model.1: 4 of 5 were red, so it is fitting to guess there are more red marbles. But blue also came up, so it is certain that there are blue marbles in it.
z-m-06-08.s.s1.hint.0: For each choice, check one by one whether this result could come out when you draw 5 times from such a bag.
z-m-06-08.s.s2.because.model.2: It is likely that there are more red marbles, but we cannot be sure. This result could come out even if there were only 1 red marble.

z-m-06-09.title: Can we decide Thursday from the records of three days in the table?
z-m-06-09.topic: Record table: guessing the next value from the first records
z-m-06-09.goal: Know that the first few values in a record table alone can't fix the next value to one, and fix Doyun's word 'must.'
z-m-06-09.material: We measure a sprout's height every morning and write it in a table. Monday 1cm, Tuesday 2cm, Wednesday 4cm. There is no Thursday record yet. Doyun said, "The increases were 1 and 2, so next it will increase by 3, so Thursday is 7cm," and Harin said, "Every day it doubles from the day before, so Thursday is 8cm."
z-m-06-09.thinking.0: Know that several rules can fit the same data
z-m-06-09.thinking.1: Distinguish a guess from a conclusion
z-m-06-09.thinking.2: Fix a friend's statement using evidence
z-m-06-09.prereq.0: Reading tables and comparing the sizes of numbers (Grade 2 level)
z-m-06-09.s.s1.prompt: With only the records of the three days in the table, can we decide whose statement is right?
z-m-06-09.s.s1.hint.0: Make the values from Monday to Wednesday with Doyun's rule and compare them with the table.
z-m-06-09.s.s1.hint.1: Do the same with Harin's rule, and set the two results side by side.
z-m-06-09.s.s1.o.d: Both are wrong. Sprouts can't be predicted.
z-m-06-09.s.s1.r.d: From the fact that predictions can be wrong, you jumped to saying all predictions are useless.
z-m-06-09.s.s1.explain: Doyun's rule continues 1, 2, 4, 7, and Harin's rule continues 1, 2, 4, 8. Both rules fit the table from Monday to Wednesday. So with these three boxes alone, we can't decide whose statement is right.
z-m-06-09.s.s2.prompt: Read the lines Doyun said afterward one by one and choose the line that was asserted without evidence.
z-m-06-09.s.s2.hint.0: Give each line a name: whether it is a record so far, a guess, or a conclusion.
z-m-06-09.s.s2.hint.1: Tell apart whether a value written in the table is a record that already exists or a value I wrote in advance.
z-m-06-09.s.s2.line.1: The increases were 1 and 2, so next it seems it will increase by 3.
z-m-06-09.s.s2.line.2: Then Thursday is 4 plus 3, so it becomes 7cm.
z-m-06-09.s.s2.line.3: I wrote 7cm in the table, so Thursday must be 7cm.
z-m-06-09.s.s2.explain: Line 4 is the line asserted without evidence. Line 2 said 'it seems' as a guess, and line 3 is a calculation that it becomes 7 if that guess is right. But in line 4, the guess was changed into 'must.' If you chose line 3, check that the calculation gives 7 only on the condition that the guess is right.
z-m-06-09.s.s3.prompt: Write what you would say to Doyun, who says 'Thursday must be 7cm' before the Thursday record comes out. Include at least one number from the table.
z-m-06-09.s.s3.hint.0: Put Doyun's statement and Harin's statement side by side and write what is the same and what is different.
z-m-06-09.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what Doyun should check before he says 'must.'
z-m-06-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say separately which part of Doyun's statement is right and which part goes too far?
z-m-06-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you include that the value can differ because of another rule?
z-m-06-09.s.s3.model.0: It could be 7cm, but if it doubles like Harin said, it is 8cm. Looking only at 1, 2, 4, we can't yet say 'must.'
z-m-06-09.s.s3.model.1: We can know only by measuring on Thursday. Just because the increases were 1 and 2, it isn't certain that the next is 3.
z-m-06-09.s.s1.o.a: Harin is right. The rule of doubling is simpler.
z-m-06-09.s.s1.r.a: You said it was right just because the rule is simple. A simple rule is not always right.
z-m-06-09.s.s1.o.b: We cannot decide. Both rules fit the records.
z-m-06-09.s.s1.r.b: You tried each of the two rules on the Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday records and noticed that both fit.
z-m-06-09.s.s1.o.c: Doyun is right. He spoke by working out the amount of increase.
z-m-06-09.s.s1.r.c: You only checked whether Doyun's rule fits the Monday to Wednesday records. You did not check whether Harin's rule fits too.
z-m-06-09.s.s3.model.2: From Monday 1, Tuesday 2, Wednesday 4, I don't know if the next one is 7 or 8. Let's look at the Thursday record before we say.
z-m-06-09.s.s3.model.3: We don't know that the one after 4 will be 7. As Harin said, 8 is possible too.

z-m-06-10.title: Which group read more books?
z-m-06-10.topic: Comparing data: a whole group and one person's share
z-m-06-10.goal: When comparing two groups with different numbers of people, know that the total number of books for the group and the number of books one person read tell different things, and make your own case where the two comparisons give different results.
z-m-06-10.material: We surveyed the number of books two groups in our class read this month. Group 가 has 3 people and Group 나 has 8 people. Everyone in Group 가 read the same number of books, and everyone in Group 나 also read the same number of books. The total number of books for a group is the number of books one person read added as many times as there are people in the group. Somi said, "Group 나 has more people, so the group that read more books is Group 나," and Jihu said, "Looking at one person at a time, a Group 가 friend might have read more."
z-m-06-10.thinking.1: Make cases that give different results yourself
z-m-06-10.thinking.2: Tell two stories from the same data
z-m-06-10.prereq.0: Calculation up to two-digit numbers and comparing the sizes of numbers (Grade 2 level)
z-m-06-10.s.s1.prompt: How can we look at what Somi said and what Jihu said?
z-m-06-10.s.s1.hint.0: In one sentence, say 'the number of what' Somi and Jihu are each comparing.
z-m-06-10.s.s1.hint.1: Decide how many books one person read, add it as many times as there are people in the group, and write the total number of books for the group.
z-m-06-10.s.s1.o.a: Only Somi is right. The group with more people also reads more books.
z-m-06-10.s.s1.r.a: You thought that if there are more people there are always more books. You didn't examine how many books one person read.
z-m-06-10.s.s1.o.b: The two statements compare different things. A whole group and one person are different.
z-m-06-10.s.s1.r.b: You pointed out that the total number of books in a group and the number of books one person read are different comparisons.
z-m-06-10.s.s1.o.c: Only Jihu is right. The number of people has nothing to do with the number of books.
z-m-06-10.s.s1.r.c: You missed that the number of people affects the total number of books for the group.
z-m-06-10.s.s1.o.d: Both are wrong. If you don't know the number of books, you can't compare.
z-m-06-10.s.s1.r.d: If you don't know the number of books, you can't state exact values, but you can say what cases are possible.
z-m-06-10.s.s1.explain: Somi is talking about the total number of books the whole group read, and Jihu is talking about the number of books one person read. Even if the group with more people read more as a whole, looking at one person at a time, the group with fewer people may have read more.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.prompt: In Group 가 each person read g books, and in Group 나 each person read h books (g and h are natural numbers from 1 to 9). Make 2 different (g, h) for which both what Somi said and what Jihu said are true. ① As a whole group, Group 나 read more books than Group 가. ② Looking at one person at a time, a Group 가 friend read more than a Group 나 friend.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.hint.0: Choose the number of books one person read so that Group 가 has more than Group 나, then find the total number of books for each whole group and compare.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.hint.1: If Group 나 is not ahead in total books, think about which side's number to change.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.var.g: Number of books one person in Group 가 read
z-m-06-10.s.s2.var.h: Number of books one person in Group 나 read
z-m-06-10.s.s2.ok.c1: Both numbers are natural numbers from 1 to 9.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.fail.c1: Make g and h natural numbers from 1 to 9.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.ok.c2: As a whole group, Group 나 read more.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.fail.c2: As a whole group, Group 나 must have more. Group 가 has 3 people and Group 나 has 8 people.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.ok.c3: Looking at one person at a time, Group 가 read more.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.fail.c3: Looking at one person at a time, Group 가 must have more than Group 나.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.explain: For example, if one person in Group 가 read 4 books and one person in Group 나 read 3 books, Group 가's total is 4 books each for 3 people, and Group 나's total is 3 books each for 8 people. Then Group 나 has more as a whole group, but one person at a time, Group 가 has more.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.because.prompt: Write what Somi and Jihu are each comparing, and why both statements can be true.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.because.hint.0: In your example, write the total number of books for Group 가 and the total number of books for Group 나.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.because.hint.1: In the same example, compare which group has more books read by one person each.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you tell apart which number Somi's statement and Jihu's statement are each about?
z-m-06-10.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you check that both statements are true with the (g, h) you made?
z-m-06-10.s.s2.because.model.0: Somi compared by putting together the books the whole group read, and Jihu compared the number of books one person read. So different results can come out.
z-m-06-10.s.s2.because.model.1: Group 나 has many people, so its total number of books can be large, but one person's share can be larger in Group 가.

z-m-06-11.title: Which list of choices is good for a survey on how students come to school?
z-m-06-11.topic: Survey: overlap and gaps when making a list of choices
z-m-06-11.goal: Know that a survey's list of choices must not overlap and must handle missing cases so every friend can mark exactly one, and find and fix problems in a list of choices.
z-m-06-11.material: Class 3 of Grade 2 is surveying 'how you come to school.' Each person marks only the one way they use most often. We thought of three lists of choices. (가) on foot, bus, subway, other ways (나) on foot, bus, subway, bicycle, car (다) on foot, vehicle, bus, bicycle. We don't yet know what ways the friends in this class actually use. There could be friends who ride a scooter or a village bus.
z-m-06-11.thinking.1: Find a way to handle missing cases
z-m-06-11.s.s1.prompt: Which list of choices lets each person pick one and mark exactly one box?
z-m-06-11.s.s1.r.d: You didn't examine whether each list has overlaps or missing cases.
z-m-06-11.s.s1.explain: (가) does not overlap, and whatever way is used, a friend can mark one box. (나) can be used only if you know in advance that the friends in this class use only one of the five ways. (다) has vehicle overlapping with bus and bicycle, so one person can fit two boxes.
z-m-06-11.s.s2.prompt: Give one example of how a friend who has trouble marking on list (다) comes to school, and write how it would be good to fix list (다).
z-m-06-11.s.s2.hint.0: Find and write a case in list (다) where the same friend has two boxes they could mark.
z-m-06-11.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether that friend can mark just one box with the fixed list.
z-m-06-11.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check with your example that one person fits two boxes?
z-m-06-11.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is your way of fixing it one that removes the overlap?
z-m-06-11.s.s2.model.0: A friend who comes by bus can mark both 'vehicle' and 'bus,' so it's confusing. 'Vehicle' includes both bus and bicycle, so one of them should be removed.
z-m-06-11.s.s2.model.1: A friend who comes by bicycle fits both vehicle and bicycle, so they overlap. Remove 'vehicle' and put in 'other ways.'
z-m-06-11.s.s3.prompt: We surveyed with list (가) and 'other ways' came out the most. What would be good to do before announcing the survey result?
z-m-06-11.s.s3.hint.0: Think about what information is missing in the survey result because many answered 'other ways.'
z-m-06-11.s.s3.o.a: Announce the result as it is, saying other ways was the most.
z-m-06-11.s.s3.r.a: You announced without knowing what ways are in other ways. It is hard for the readers of the announcement to understand.
z-m-06-11.s.s3.o.b: Erase the other ways box and announce comparing only the remaining boxes.
z-m-06-11.s.s3.r.b: You erased the box with the most answers. The largest part of the answers of the friends surveyed would be missing.
z-m-06-11.s.s3.o.c: Ask the other friends what ways they use and divide them again.
z-m-06-11.s.s3.r.c: This is the idea of dividing up the inside of other ways again to find out which ways are common.
z-m-06-11.s.s3.o.d: Redo the whole survey from the beginning and announce it fresh.
z-m-06-11.s.s3.r.d: You threw away all the results already collected. Think about whether it is enough to find out again only the other ways box.
z-m-06-11.s.s3.explain: If other ways was the most, it would be good to find out which ways are common inside it. If you ask only the friends in that box and divide them again, you can use the results already collected without throwing them away.
z-m-06-11.s.s3.acc.0: Redoing the survey from the beginning is also a method, but it is more fitting to use the results already obtained and find out again only the missing part.
z-m-06-11.s.s1.hint.0: For each list, check one by one whether a friend who comes by kick scooter has a cell to mark.
z-m-06-11.s.s1.hint.1: For each list, count whether a person has one cell or two or more cells they could mark.
z-m-06-11.s.s1.r.a: You missed that bus and bicycle are included in vehicle, so one person could fit in two cells.
z-m-06-11.s.s1.r.b: You looked at the point that the cells do not overlap and that a way that is left out can be marked under "other ways".
z-m-06-11.s.s1.r.c: The five ways do not overlap with each other. But think about where a friend who uses a kick scooter or a village bus would mark.
z-m-06-11.s.s2.model.2: A friend who comes by bus can mark both vehicle and bus. Remove vehicle and make cells for subway and car.
z-m-06-11.s.s3.hint.1: Write down which friends need to be surveyed again and how the results already collected can be used.
